# Smaraṇa and Bhakti-Samādhi vs Kaivalya

## Two Climbers, One Staircase: The Empty Room and the Face

Picture two people climbing the exact same staircase. Same steps, same handrail, same number of landings, same burn in the legs. One of them is climbing toward a room at the top that is perfectly empty — white walls, no furniture, no sound, just a clean silence that is somehow the most restful thing they have ever felt. The other is climbing the same stairs toward a room where someone they love is waiting, and the whole climb is sweet because of who's at the top.

That's the whole argument of this page in one image. The staircase is the meditative ladder that classical yoga built — pull your attention off the world, narrow it to a single point, sink into that point until your sense of "me sitting here watching" dissolves. Patañjali built that staircase. The Bhāgavata tradition climbs it step for step. But where Patañjali's climber is heading for the empty white room — pure awareness resting in its own nature, nobody home, no object — the bhakta is heading for a face. Kṛṣṇa. A person. Blue like a storm cloud, holding a flute.[^1]

Same architecture. Opposite destination. And the tradition makes a claim that should stop you cold: the people who actually reached the empty white room — the fully realized sages — *came back down the stairs on purpose* to keep climbing toward the face instead.[^2] The silence wasn't enough. They wanted the person more.

The Sanskrit word at the center of all this is **smaraṇa** — "remembering." Hold Kṛṣṇa in your mind without a break. That's the practice. And according to Jīva Gosvāmin, the great systematizer of this tradition, that constant remembering isn't one practice among nine — it's the *actual goal* of the entire devotional system.[^3]

## What Smaraṇa Actually Is: The Goal Hiding Inside the Method

The path of devotional practice has nine steps. The first is **śravaṇa**, hearing — you listen to the stories of God, and that plants a seed. The second is **kīrtana**, chanting — you sing the names, and that scrubs the mind clean of the noise that competes for it. But the third step, smaraṇa, is different in kind from the two before it. Hearing initiates. Chanting purifies. Remembering is the thing the other two were *for*.[^3]

Jīva pins the definition to a single verse of the Bhāgavata: "Yoga has been taught as being that by which the mind is withdrawn from everything else, and fixed on Me."[^4] Read that slowly. That is not a definition of devotion. That is a definition of *yoga* — pulling the mind off everything and parking it on one thing. The only edit the tradition makes is the identity of the one thing. For Patañjali the "one thing" can be almost anything you steady the mind on; the goal lies past all objects, in awareness alone. For the bhakta the one thing is always, only, a person.

Here's why this matters and isn't just sectarian flag-waving. Smaraṇa is "remembering Kṛṣṇa at all times" — not for an hour on a cushion but as the standing condition of your mind, the way you might carry a worry or a love through an ordinary day without ever consciously summoning it.[^5] The Gītā keeps hammering this. "Of all yogīs, the one who performs devotion to Me with his innermost self absorbed in Me is the best of all."[^6] "Fix your mind on Me and become My devotee."[^7] The whole machinery — the hearing, the chanting, the deity worship that comes later — exists to make this one thing possible: a mind that never lets go of God.

And there's a prerequisite, which is why the order of the nine matters. You can't keep Kṛṣṇa in your thoughts if your thoughts are a swamp of cravings and grudges. Jīva says remembrance is only possible once the heart is clean — which is exactly the job chanting did one step back.[^8] You scour the surface first. Then you can write on it.

## The Ladder Inside the Ladder: Jīva's Five Steps and Patañjali's Top Three

Now the mechanism gets precise, and this is where the page earns its keep. Jīva doesn't leave smaraṇa as a vague "think about God a lot." He builds it into a five-step sequence — and that sequence is, almost beam for beam, the top of Patañjali's eight-limbed yoga ladder with a devotional skin stretched over it.[^9]

Walk up it. **Step one** is smaraṇa itself — bring Kṛṣṇa to mind however your temperament inclines. **Step two** is **dhāraṇā**, which is also Patañjali's sixth limb: pull the mind off the world and aim it at God in a general way — concentration, holding. **Step three** is **dhyāna**, Patañjali's seventh limb: settle into sustained contemplation, dwelling on Kṛṣṇa's name, form, qualities, and deeds — meditation proper. **Step four** is **dhruvānusmṛti**, "fixed remembrance," a flow of awareness running unbroken like a continuous pour of nectar — Jīva slots this one *between* Patañjali's limbs, his own devotional addition. **Step five** is **samādhi**, Patañjali's eighth and final limb: the state where only the object remains and the sense of a separate self watching it falls away entirely.[^9]

Lay the two ladders side by side and they're the same ladder. Concentration, meditation, absorption. The motor is identical. This is why Bryant can call Patañjali's brief recommendation to meditate on Īśvara "Bhakti Lite" and the Bhāgavata's full devotional system "Bhakti Extra-Strength" — they aren't two different drugs, they're two doses of the same one.[^10] Patañjali mentions God as the best single object to steady the mind on and then walks past Him toward the impersonal goal. The Bhāgavata takes that same recommendation and refuses to walk past.

But the fifth step is where the ladders, having shared every rung, point at two different rooms. In Patañjali's system the final absorption empties out toward **svarūpa** — awareness resting in its own nature, the self knowing only itself, no object at all. That's **kaivalya**, "aloneness," the contentless white room.[^11] In bhakti-samādhi the object never disappears. At the top of the climb the bhakta doesn't dissolve into objectless silence — they get a direct vision of Kṛṣṇa as a real, distinct Being, a personal form made of pure consciousness, standing present before their awareness.[^12] Not a mental picture anymore. The actual person.

So the destabilizing claim is structural, not decorative. It isn't that bhakti is a warmer flavor of the same trip. It's that the identical meditative machine, run to completion, can deliver you to two opposite places — an empty self or a present God — and which one you reach depends entirely on what you aimed the machine at on the way up.

## What This Gives the Vault: A Shared Engine With a Contested Exit

This page hands the vault a clean structural tool: a single meditative architecture that two traditions share completely and use to reach opposite ends. That's rare and useful. Most cross-tradition comparisons are loose family resemblances. This one is exact — Jīva *names* Patañjali's limbs and adopts them by number.[^9]

For the yoga pages, this sharpens what [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/dharana-dhyana-samadhi-samyama|Dhāraṇā, Dhyāna, Samādhi (Saṃyama)]] is actually doing. Saṃyama — the fused threefold of concentration-meditation-absorption — turns out to be substrate, not destination. It's the engine block. Bolt the impersonal self onto it and you get kaivalya; bolt Kṛṣṇa onto it and you get bhakti-samādhi. The technique is theologically neutral; only the object is contested.

For the liberation pages, this complicates [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/models-of-liberation-the-mokshakaraka-survey|Models of Liberation (the Mokṣakāraka Survey)]] from inside. The survey catalogues different *destinations* of liberation. Smaraṇa shows that two of those destinations can be reached by the *same road*, which means the difference between them was never a difference of method — it was a difference of desire. That reframes the whole survey: the models aren't competing techniques, they're competing answers to "what do you most want at the top of the stairs?"

And it feeds the bhakti cluster directly. The sibling pages — [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/bhakti-as-classical-yoga-in-reverse|Bhakti as Classical Yoga in Reverse]], [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/the-nine-practices-of-vaidhi-bhakti|The Nine Practices of Vaidhī Bhakti]], [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/bhakti-minimizes-moksa|Bhakti Minimizes Mokṣa]] — all lean on the claim made here: that the personal vision outranks impersonal liberation in this tradition's own value-order, and that the proof is sages voluntarily climbing back down.

## Analytical Case Study: Vyāsa Walks Back Down the Stairs

The cleanest evidence the tradition offers is the case of Vyāsa, the sage credited with compiling the Vedas — and it's a strange, almost scandalous little episode if you take liberation seriously.

Vyāsa had arrived. The text is explicit: "he was fixed in the bliss of the self and was devoid of any other thought."[^13] That's it. That's the goal of generic yoga, achieved. He's in the white room. The mind is empty of everything but its own nature, resting in the bliss of pure awareness — exactly what Patañjali's whole eight-limbed ladder was built to deliver. By the standards of kaivalya, there is nowhere higher to go and nothing more to want.

And then the verse turns: "his heart was attracted to the enchanting līlās of the infallible Kṛṣṇa."[^13] Read that against where he's standing. He is *inside* the supreme silence, the self-bliss that the entire yogic tradition treats as the summit — and his heart pulls *down*, back toward stories, toward a person doing things, toward Kṛṣṇa's playful deeds. The bliss of the self, it turns out, has a ceiling he can feel. He wants the face more than the empty room.

So Nārada gives him an instruction that should sound impossible: "recall, by means of samādhi, the activities of Kṛṣṇa."[^14] Look at what that sentence asks. *Use samādhi* — the deepest meditative absorption, the very state classical yoga reserves for dissolving into objectless awareness — and aim it not at emptiness but at Kṛṣṇa's specific, narrative, embodied deeds. Take the most rarefied tool in the kit and point it at a story. Vyāsa does, and "in his mind, which, completely purified by the practice of bhakti yoga, was fully concentrated, he saw that perfect Person."[^15] The fifth stage. Not an idea of God assembled from memory-impressions, but the direct vision — the face, present.

Here's the deconstruction. In a kaivalya framework Vyāsa's move is a *regression*. He had the objectless goal in hand and he traded it for an object, went back from formless to form, from silence to story. The whole point of yoga, on Patañjali's reading, is to get past objects; Vyāsa got past them and then deliberately reinstalled one. The tradition knows exactly how this looks and embraces it anyway, because for the Bhāgavata the "regression" is the actual ascent. The empty room was a landing, not the top. Śuka, Vyāsa's son, is invoked the same way — already self-realized, still pulled into Kṛṣṇa's pastimes.[^16] The pattern is the argument: the people most qualified to stay in the silence are the ones who keep choosing the face.

That's what makes the case study load-bearing rather than illustrative. You can dismiss a beginner preferring devotion as not knowing what they're missing. You cannot say that about a sage who is demonstrably *in* the impersonal bliss and walks back down on purpose. The tradition has stacked the deck with its strongest possible witness.

## Implementation Workflow: A Day Held by One Thread

It's late and you're lying in the dark, and the day replays itself without your asking — a thing someone said, a worry about tomorrow, a song stuck on loop. Notice that your mind does this on its own. It's *always* remembering something. Smaraṇa isn't asking you to install a new faculty. It's asking you to change what the always-running remembering is running on.

Morning. Before the day's noise arrives you sit, and the first move isn't concentration — it's chanting, the step before. The names go around and around until the swamp drains a little, until there's a clear surface to write on. Only then does the mind have room to hold a single thing steady. You feel the difference physically: the grudge you carried in with you has loosened its grip, and into that loosened space the form can come.

| What the mind does on its own | What smaraṇa redirects it toward |
|---|---|
| Replays an argument | Replays a deed of Kṛṣṇa — the flute, the cows, the bower |
| Rehearses tomorrow's worry | Holds a single form: blue like a storm cloud, ornaments, gesture |
| Drifts to the empty self in deep meditation | Lets the object stay; aims the absorption *at* the person, not past Him |
| Wants quiet | Wants the face, and finds quiet on the way as a side effect |

Now the form. You're not summoning God out of thin air — the senses can't reach Him directly, so you build the image out of what you already have. Blue you've seen in monsoon sky. A flute you've heard. The deeds you've heard read aloud, standardized by repetition until they're vivid and shared.[^17] This is why the Bhāgavata pours out such lavish physical description of Kṛṣṇa's body and ornaments — it's handing you the raw material to build with. (This is the seam where this page meets [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/smarana-as-imaginative-construction|Smaraṇa as Imaginative Construction]]: the form is, at first, a thing made of mind-stuff.)

Then the day. The thread of remembrance pays out behind you while you work, the way a melody you love hums under everything without your performing it. Dhāraṇā is the morning grip; dhyāna is the dwelling that deepens through the day; dhruvānusmṛti is when the thread stops snapping — an unbroken pour, nectar that doesn't gap. And on the rare height, samādhi: the watcher drops away and only the beloved object stands there. You'll know you've crossed from constructed-form into vision when the form stops being *yours* — stops being a picture you're holding up — and simply *is there*, present in front of your awareness like another person in the room.

## The Smaraṇa Failure: A Picture You're Holding Up by Hand

The failure mode is subtle because the practice looks identical whether it's working or collapsing. You're sitting, you're "remembering Kṛṣṇa," and from the outside nothing's wrong. From inside, here's the rot.

**The slideshow that never warms.** You can build the form perfectly — blue, flute, ornaments, the whole gallery — and have it stay dead. A wax figure. The text is blunt about the cure: the mentally constructed form only comes alive, only carries personal presence, if the effort is *permeated with bhakti*.[^18] Without the love, smaraṇa is just lucid daydreaming about a blue man. The diagnostic sign is that you're impressed by your own visualization. If the imaging feels like a skill you're performing, the warmth hasn't arrived and you've mistaken vividness for presence.

**Trying to hold the thread on a dirty surface.** You skip the chanting, the purification, and try to jump straight to constant remembrance — and the form keeps getting shouldered aside by the grudge, the craving, the replay. Jīva's order isn't a suggestion. Remembrance on an unscrubbed mind is two cars fighting for one lane; the louder, older traffic wins.[^8]

**Climbing toward the wrong room without noticing.** This is the deep one. You can run the entire five-step ladder and, at the top, let the object thin out into objectless silence because that's the famous goal you absorbed from every other yoga teaching. You reach kaivalya by reflex. Nothing has gone wrong by Patañjali's lights — but by the Bhāgavata's, you've walked past the face into the empty room out of sheer habit. The sign is a samādhi that goes quiet and contentless and *peaceful* rather than overwhelming and personal. For this tradition, peace at the summit is the symptom: the real thing is closer to what happens to Caitanya, where the body can barely survive the dose.[^19]

## Samādhi With a Seed in It

The two-rooms picture assumes both climbers reach the same height and turn different ways at the top. A second scheme says they don't get to the same height at all, and the reason sits inside what a support does.

Sort the eight absorptions into two sets of four. The first four reach the Realm of Form, and they're grouped that way because they still run on a **support** — something the mind is held against. The Vedantan name for this set is *samprajñāta samādhi*, absorption with support. Two further names say it more bluntly: *sālambana* samādhi, with-support, and ***bīja* samādhi — samādhi with a seed in it.**[^20]

The seed isn't decorative there. It's the technical claim: an absorption cultivated against a mental support **produces tendencies, seeds for future functions of consciousness.**[^20] You come out of it with something planted.

The second four are specified by subtraction. Deeper states of emptiness that don't rely on form, empty of any consciousness involving objects, and hard to find the trace of a mind in at all. A method requirement comes attached, and it's stated as a requirement rather than a recommendation: **to cultivate the formless absorptions you have to follow the no-thought path.**[^20]

Put those together and the staircase grows a landing nobody mentioned. A face is a support. An absorption held on a face is a with-seed absorption, and with-seed absorptions are the first four. The last four are shut to anything that keeps an object — not because a face is the wrong object, but because holding one at all is the disqualifying move.

So on this scheme the bhakta tops out at rung four of eight, and the empty room is somewhere past rungs the devotional method can't climb by construction. Same engine. Not the same height.

It also puts the sages' descent in a harder light. Coming back down to climb toward the face is, on these terms, a move from the formless absorptions into the form realm — a drop in rank, not a lateral choice between two summits. The tradition frames it as preferring the person. The second scheme would call the same act a demotion, and neither side is arguing with the other.

## Evidence / Tensions / Open Questions

The textual spine is firm. Jīva explicitly maps his five-step smaraṇa onto Patañjali's sixth-through-eighth limbs and adds dhruvānusmṛti as his own interpolation;[^9] the Bhāgavata supplies the defining verse that frames smaraṇa as yoga proper;[^4] the Gītā supplies the "best of yogīs is the devotee" capstone.[^6] The Vyāsa episode is the tradition's chosen proof-case and it's quoted directly.[^13]

The live tension is whether the "regression" reading survives scrutiny or whether it's special pleading. A skeptic says: of course the devotional tradition tells a story where the impersonal sage wants the personal God — that's the conclusion it needs, dressed as evidence. Vyāsa "preferring" the līlās could be a theological device, not a report. The tradition's answer is that it picked the *hardest* possible witness — a fully self-realized sage, not a beginner — precisely to forestall the "they don't know what they're missing" dismissal. Whether that's a genuine argument or a more sophisticated form of the same circularity is left open here, and it's the kind of question the [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/models-of-liberation-the-mokshakaraka-survey|Mokṣakāraka Survey]] is built to adjudicate.

A second, quieter tension: Bryant writes as both academic Indologist and Gauḍīya practitioner, and the claim that bhakti-bliss "far eclipses" the bliss of the self is stated as the *bhāgavatas claim*[^12] — the tradition's own valuation, not a neutral finding. This page documents that valuation; it does not endorse the sectarian ranking of bhakti over kaivalya as settled fact.

Open: is bhakti-samādhi a *different state* from kaivalya, or the *same state* differently described from inside a relationship? The text insists the object genuinely persists in bhakti-samādhi where it vanishes in kaivalya — a real structural difference, not a mood. But whether that can be verified from the outside, or only asserted from within, stays unresolved.

## Author Tensions & Convergences

Bryant and Patañjali don't actually disagree about how the mind works — that's what makes their split so sharp. Patañjali, as Bryant reads him through Jīva, hands over the whole technology of absorption: withdraw the mind, narrow it, sink it, lose the watcher. Bryant takes every piece of that and changes nothing about the mechanism. So when they part ways at the summit it isn't a quarrel about method. It's a quarrel about what the method is *for*. Patañjali wants the practitioner emptied out into pure awareness; Bryant's tradition wants the practitioner filled up with a present God. The split tells you something neither says alone: the technique of meditation is morally and theologically blank. It will take you wherever you were already pointed. The destination was never in the staircase — it was in the climber's wanting.

Set this against Vivekananda, who runs through the vault's [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/models-of-liberation-the-mokshakaraka-survey|liberation survey]] as a voice that tends to fold the personal God up into the impersonal Absolute as a lower rung you eventually outgrow. Bryant inverts the ladder. For Vivekananda the personal is the scaffolding and the impersonal is the building; for Bryant's Vyāsa the impersonal is the landing you stand on briefly before climbing toward the personal, which is the actual top. Both are using the same vertical metaphor — higher and lower, more and less — and they've swapped which end is which. What that reveals: "higher" in these traditions is never a fact about consciousness. It's a verdict about value, smuggled in wearing the clothes of altitude.

And against the vault's Tantric voices — Wallis especially — there's a convergence worth naming. Both Bryant's Bhāgavata and Wallis's non-dual Śaivism refuse to treat the world-of-objects as something to be escaped into a blank. Both keep the form. But they keep it for different reasons: the Tantric keeps form because the world *is* the deity's own self-display, so there's nothing to leave; Bryant keeps form because the deity is a *person* you'd be heartbroken to lose into silence. One keeps the object out of metaphysics, the other out of love. The shared refusal of the empty room, reached by two completely different routes, suggests the impersonal absolute may be less the consensus summit of Indian thought than the textbooks imply — more like one option among several that several major traditions actively decline.

## Cross-Domain Handshakes

Here's the plain reason these domains connect: smaraṇa is, in the tradition's own words, a *mental construct* built out of the same stuff every other thought is built from — leftover impressions of things you've seen and heard — which means the practice is doing, with sacred intent, exactly what cognitive psychology studies when it studies mental imagery and attention.[^17]

- **Psychology**: [[ARCHIVES/concepts/psychology/phantasy-and-imagination|Phantasy and Imagination]] — The structural identity is almost uncomfortable. Bryant says the divine form you meditate on is assembled from saṃskāras — impressions of prior sense experience — because the senses can't reach God directly, so you build Him from blue skies you've seen and flutes you've heard.[^17] That is mental imagery in the strict psychological sense: a percept-like experience with no present stimulus, stitched from memory. The tension is where they aim. Psychology treats the constructed image as the endpoint — the image *is* the phenomenon. Bryant treats the constructed image as a *transitional object* that, if soaked in devotion, gets superseded by something the construction was only ever standing in for: a direct presence that is no longer made of saṃskāras at all.[^12] The insight that neither field reaches alone: a deliberately constructed mental image can function as scaffolding for a state the image itself doesn't contain — which would mean visualization practices aren't valuable because the picture is accurate, but because holding *any* sufficiently loved picture trains a faculty that eventually operates without it. That reframes guided visualization across every therapeutic and contemplative context: the image is a trellis, not the plant.

- **Psychology**: [[ARCHIVES/concepts/psychology/self-image-thinking-visualization|Self-Image Thinking (Visualization)]] — Self-image work holds a vivid picture of a desired self until behavior reorganizes around it; the picture is a tool for becoming. Smaraṇa holds a vivid picture of the beloved God until the mind reorganizes around *Him* — same mechanic, repetition building a standing mental object that bends the rest of cognition toward it. The split is the direction of the pull. Self-image thinking pulls the picture *into* you — you become the image. Smaraṇa pulls *you* toward the picture — you don't become Kṛṣṇa, you arrive in front of Him; the goal is relationship, not identity, and the tradition is fierce that the bhakta and Kṛṣṇa stay two. What that exposes: visualization techniques quietly split into two families by what they do with the gap between viewer and image. Close the gap and you get transformation-of-self. Preserve the gap and you get devotion. Most modern visualization assumes closing the gap is the point — smaraṇa shows that *keeping* it is a coherent and possibly higher-yield alternative, because a beloved object you never merge with is one you can keep wanting forever, and the wanting is the fuel.

- **Psychology**: [[ARCHIVES/concepts/psychology/unwavering-focus|Unwavering Focus]] — Dhruvānusmṛti, Jīva's "fixed remembrance flowing without interruption like a continuous pour of nectar," is sustained attention with no lapse — the exact thing attention research measures as the failure of mind-wandering to occur.[^9] The parallel is clean; the tension is what sustains the focus. Secular attention training fights mind-wandering with effort and meta-awareness — you catch the drift and haul back. Smaraṇa doesn't fight it; it makes the object *more interesting than the wandering* by loving it, so the mind stops wandering the way you stop checking your phone when someone you adore is talking. The insight neither frame produces alone: unbroken attention may be cheaper to buy with love than with discipline. Effortful focus exhausts; affectionate focus self-feeds. That predicts something testable — that attention sustained by genuine attraction should fatigue far slower than attention sustained by willpower, which reframes the entire project of "focus training" as possibly a misallocated effort that should be spent cultivating attraction instead.

## The Live Edge

**The Sharpest Implication**

You probably assume that the highest spiritual state is some version of peace — emptiness, stillness, the quiet mind, the dissolving of the self into a calm vastness. Almost every meditation app, every popular account of enlightenment, every "letting go" framing points at the empty white room as the top of the stairs. This concept says: that's a *choice*, not a summit. The exact same staircase reaches a different room, and the tradition's most accomplished climbers — the ones who actually got to the peace — walked back down out of it on purpose because the peace had a ceiling they could feel. If they're right, then the contentless calm you've been told is the goal might be the place you pass through, and the thing you do when you get there — choosing the silence — might be the reflex you mistook for arrival. The uncomfortable part: you can't tell from where you're sitting whether you'd choose the empty room or the face, because you've never been offered the face. You've only been trained to climb toward empty.

**Generative Questions**

- If the meditative technique is theologically blank and only the *object* decides the destination, what determines which object a practitioner can actually love enough to sustain — and is that capacity for devotion the real, untaught prerequisite that no method can install?
- The tradition's proof is a realized sage choosing the personal God over the impersonal self. What would the *symmetrical* proof look like — a realized bhakta abandoning the face for the silence — and does its apparent absence in the literature reveal something real, or just whose books survived?
- If love sustains attention more cheaply than discipline (per the unwavering-focus handshake), is every effort-based contemplative and productivity practice quietly inefficient — solving an attraction problem with a willpower tool?

# The Corpus Inverts the Most Famous Image for Generosity in the Tradition

## Somebody Asks for Help

The second of the three prohibitions is stated flatly and then given a situation:

> Do not use your spiritual energies on the other **without proper permission.** If your guru has not given you permission, **do not interfere.**[^1]

The situation is ordinary and well observed. Two practitioners are talking. One says his life is full of suffering, that the other has been practising a long time, and *can you not use your spiritual power to help me? Please come to my home. Come and sit, spend some time.*[^2]

And the response the teacher describes isn't greed. It's something better disguised:

> That disciple felt something awaken within him. He thought: **my positiveness — people are able to feel it. My presence is making a difference to people. Let me go there.**[^3]

⚑ Note where the temptation is located. It's not in the helping. It's in the sentence *my presence is making a difference*, which arrives as an observation and functions as an appointment. This material's whole warning is aimed at the moment a capacity is noticed and immediately becomes an office.

## The Guru's First Answer, Which Is Not About Depletion

The disciple does the correct thing — he goes and asks permission. And the first thing said to him isn't about running out:

> Who told you that **what has been gathered in your sādhanā belongs to [you]?**[^4]

That's an ownership claim, not a conservation one. On this answer the objection to giving it away is that it was never yours to give, and depletion is beside the point. A steward who distributes what he holds in trust hasn't been imprudent; he has exceeded his authority.

The teacher never returns to this line and it's the strongest one in the passage.

## The Image, and What Is Odd About It

Then the guru switches arguments:

> When a lamp is lit in your house — **can you give away its entire flame and still expect your lamp to remain burning?** A lamp to remain burning cannot happen.[^5]

⚠️ This is an inversion of the most widely used image for generosity in this tradition and in several others. The familiar version runs the other way: a lamp loses nothing by lighting another lamp; a thousand can be lit from one and the first burns undiminished. It's the standard illustration of why knowledge, teaching and blessing aren't depleted by being shared.

The teacher's version requires the transfer to be total — *its entire flame* — and with that qualifier the sentence is true. But the qualifier is doing all the work, and it's doing it silently. Nobody who asks a practitioner for help is asking for their entire flame. The scenario the episode has just described is a man asking someone to come and sit in his house.

⚑ This build doesn't claim the inversion is deliberate. What can be said is that this material reaches for a stock image, changes the one word that reverses its meaning, and doesn't remark on it — and that the image's ordinary form would have supported the opposite conclusion from the one being drawn.

## The Bowl, Which Commits to Conservation

The second image has no such ambiguity:

> Your sādhanā is like water. **You have spent months gathering it.** And if you begin pouring it everywhere merely because someone asks you — every drop, every drop you're trying to pour — **one day you will discover that your own vessel is empty.**[^6]

Water is a conserved quantity. Poured out, it's gone, and the vessel doesn't refill by itself. This image commits fully to the depletion model, and the teacher backs it with a time cost: *rebuilding that inner strength can take a very long time, even years of efforts.*[^7]

⚑ So the passage contains three separate reasons for the same prohibition, and they aren't versions of one another.

1. Ownership. It's not yours. — *Who told you that what has been gathered belongs to you?*
2. Conservation. You'll run out. — the bowl, and the years of rebuilding.
3. Karmic entanglement. You'll take on what's theirs. — *some people bring their karmas to cleanse it. Do not become part of their karma.*[^8]

These have different implications for the same case. On (1) the practitioner may not give even from abundance. On (2) they may give once they have enough. On (3) the danger isn't what leaves them but what arrives, and the transaction runs the opposite way.

Not resolved here. The passage states all three inside ninety seconds and treats them as one point.

## Compassion Is Good, Interference Is Not

The line the passage is built to deliver is the crispest thing in the episode:

> **Compassion is good. Interference is not.**[^9]

And it comes with a behavioural substitute rather than a prohibition alone, which is what makes it usable. What the sādhaka does afterwards is specified:

> He did not become a saviour. He became simple. **He prayed: let Bhairava support you, let Mā be with you.** He remained silent, and continued his own sādhanā.[^10]

⚑ That's not a refusal to help. It's a redirection of the request to a third party, with the practitioner remaining present and doing nothing. This material's answer to *can you help me* isn't *no* — it's *I will ask on your behalf*, which preserves the relationship and removes the practitioner from the mechanism.

The disposition prescribed alongside it is stated three times and doesn't soften:

> Act like a fool, as simple nonsense, telling that I don't know anything. **Stay humble, stay very silent, stay on your path.**[^11]

> Even when you feel capable, remember you are still a beginner. **Walk like a fool. Remain ordinary. No extraordinary.**[^12]

> **Someone's karma is not your mission.**[^13]

## Analytical Case Study — Which Reason Survives the Obvious Objection

Test the three reasons against the case that a critic would immediately raise: a practitioner with genuine capacity refuses to help someone who is suffering, and the suffering continues.

**Conservation does badly.** It makes the practitioner's spiritual reserves a private asset to be protected, and it produces a tradition of people accumulating something they will never spend. The teacher half-sees this — his own qualifier is *until Bhairava decides whenever your hands are [ready] to serve another*[^14] — which concedes that spending is the point and postpones it. But a doctrine that says *later* with no criterion is functionally a doctrine that says *no*.

**Karmic entanglement does better but proves too much.** If contact with another's karma is dangerous, the danger doesn't wait for a formal request. A tradition holding it seriously would have to say something about ordinary proximity, and this one doesn't.

Ownership is the one that survives, and this material abandons it after one sentence.

*What has been gathered in your sādhanā does not belong to you* answers the objection completely and without meanness. The practitioner isn't hoarding, because there's nothing to hoard; they aren't refusing, because they were never the party with standing to grant. The suffering person isn't being turned away — they're being correctly redirected to the party who does have standing, which is precisely what the prayer at 31:10 does.

⚑ And it explains the permission structure, which the other two reasons can't. If the objection were depletion, the guru's permission would be irrelevant — permission doesn't refill a bowl. If it were karmic danger, permission would be reckless. Permission only makes sense if the guru is the one with authority to disburse, which is exactly what the ownership answer implies and what the episode's own procedure enacts: the disciple doesn't decide, he goes and asks.

So the passage's structure is better than its arguments. The practice it describes — ask, be refused, redirect the request upward, stay ordinary — follows from the reason it states once and drops, and doesn't follow from the two it develops at length.

⚠️ The honest cost, stated: this is still a doctrine in which a person in distress is told that the practitioner can't help and will pray instead, and in which the practitioner's capacity is real by this material's own account. Whether the redirection is a kindness or a refusal dressed as one isn't settled by anything in the episode, and both readings survive the text.

## Implementation Workflow

Somebody you know is suffering, and you've been sitting for a while now, and the thought arrives on its own: *maybe I could do something.* That thought is the whole subject of this passage, and the instruction is to notice it and stop there.

The first move is a question with a factual answer: has your guru told you to use it for this?[^1] Not *would he approve*, not *would it help* — has he said so. If the answer is no, the passage's word is *stop*, and it doesn't soften it.[^1]

What you do instead is given, and it's deliberately small. You pray for them — *let Bhairava support you, let Mā be with you* — you stay quiet about the rest, and you go back to your own sitting.[^10] That's what the disciple in the story ends up doing, and the story presents it as the mature version rather than the disappointing one.

⚑ The sentence to keep is the one about the timing, because it takes the decision off you entirely: *Bhairava decides when your hands are meant to serve another. Until then, protect what your sādhanā has been giving you.*[^14] So this isn't a permanent prohibition on helping. It's a claim that the readiness isn't yours to assess, which is exactly why the check above is *has he said so* rather than *do I feel ready*.

⚠️ And the failure mode has a specific shape worth watching for. The disciple didn't set out to interfere; he felt something wake in him, noticed that people responded to his presence, and concluded that he was making a difference.[^2] That sequence — a real change, a real response from others, and a conclusion drawn from both — is how it starts, and every step of it feels like evidence.

The instruction that closes it is four words long and none of them is about power: *walk like a fool, remain ordinary.*[^12] Followed by the one that settles the boundary: *someone's karma is not your mission.*[^13]

## Where This Comes From

One video, published 2026-08-15, 370 lines, from the channel's usual unnamed teacher.[^15] The second mistake runs 25:02–32:34.

Ordinary English. *Sādhanā*, *satsaṅga*, *śiṣya* legible.

⚠️ At 26:01 the pair of karma-terms arrives as `pradha sanit karma` — almost certainly the prārabdha/sañcita pair this material uses elsewhere, and **not reconstructed here.** The teacher's point is legible without it: the guru is protecting the disciple from a karmic mechanism the disciple doesn't understand.

No text is cited.

## Evidence & Cautions

**What's strong.** *Compassion is good, interference is not*, and the prayer as a substitute rather than a refusal. Together they make the prohibition livable.

**What's weak.** The lamp, which inverts a stock image without acknowledging it and which needs *entire* to be true.

**Tension, preserved.** Three incompatible reasons for one prohibition, in ninety seconds.

**Open question.** *Until Bhairava decides when your hands are ready to serve another.* What's the sign? This material specifies the waiting and not the ending, and a permission with no criterion is indistinguishable from a refusal.

**Absence, stated carefully.** No text, no locator. The lamp image isn't attributed, and its more common form isn't mentioned.

## Against the Vault's Other Material

The vault holds this material's own kṛpā material from an earlier ingest of the same channel — grace as something that arrives from the deity, unearned, and characteristically in excess of what was asked for.[^16]

⚑ Kṛpā and the bowl can't both be the whole story, and the tension is worth keeping.

If what the practitioner holds is *gathered* — accumulated by months of effort, depleted by use, rebuilt over years — then it's a stock, and the bowl image is correct.

If what the practitioner holds is *kṛpā* — given, unearned, and continuing — then it's a flow, and the bowl is the wrong instrument entirely. You can't empty a channel by using it.

This material holds both, in different episodes, and the difference determines the whole question this page is about. A stock must be protected. A flow can't be.

And the ownership answer sits on the flow side: *what has been gathered does not belong to you* is much easier to say about grace than about the product of one's own months of effort. Which suggests this material's best argument and its other doctrine agree — and that the depletion imagery, which is what the episode develops, belongs to neither.

Held open.

## Cross-Domain Handshakes

Psychology — the helper who was manufactured by the helping. The vault holds **creating the helper**: the account of how a person comes to occupy the helping role, and how the role, once occupied, starts holding up their sense of who they are.[^17]

This is the mechanism this material's passage describes and can't name.

Look again at where the episode locates the temptation. Not in the request. Not in compassion. In *my presence is making a difference to people* — a self-description arriving in the moment before an action, and one that the action will then confirm.

The clinical account says what happens next: the role is self-reinforcing, because each act of helping supplies evidence for the identity that motivated it, and the identity increasingly requires the acts. What began as a capacity becomes a requirement, and a person in that position can't decline a request without a loss that has nothing to do with the person asking.

What the guru's permission is actually protecting is where the two accounts meet.

Read as the passage states it, permission protects a resource. Read through the clinical account, permission does something else and better: it keeps the decision outside the practitioner's identity. A practitioner who must ask can't accrete the role, because the role is never theirs to assume. Each time, the call is made by someone with no stake in how the practitioner sees themselves.

Which reframes the whole prohibition. It's not a rule about spiritual energy. It's a structural defence against a specific and well-documented way that helping people goes wrong — and it works by removing the one thing that makes the failure possible, which is unilateral authority to help.

That yields a transferable form: when a role confirms itself, what protects you isn't restraint — it's somebody outside making the call. Willpower fails here, because the person deciding is the person whose identity depends on the decision. What works is exactly what the episode describes — a standing requirement to ask someone who isn't invested in the answer.

## The Live Edge

**Sharpest implication.** The passage states its best argument once — *what has been gathered does not belong to you* — and develops two weaker ones at length. Only the abandoned one explains the permission structure the episode actually enacts.

**Generative questions.**

- Stock or flow? The bowl says stock and this channel's kṛpā doctrine says flow, and the whole prohibition depends on which.
- The lamp image is the tradition's standard illustration of undiminished giving, reversed by one word. Is this teacher inverting it knowingly, and does the corpus use the ordinary form anywhere?
- *Until Bhairava decides your hands are ready.* Does any episode in this corpus describe the sign, or is the permission structurally deferred?

# The Siddhis Are Māyā

## The Powers Are Real, and That Is the Problem

Sit long enough, the tradition says, and things start happening. You know what someone is about to say. You stop needing much sleep. Distances behave oddly. Whatever the mechanism, the practice throws off effects, and the effects are more interesting to talk about than the practice.

Kapila's ruling on them is nine words long and it does not deny a single one:

> O dear one! **There are siddhis obtained through yoga, but these are maya.**[^1]

*There are.* He grants the whole catalogue in the first clause. The demotion happens in the second, and it demotes them by classification rather than by disproof.

## One Clause, at the End of a Chapter

Where it sits matters. This is the last thing said in 3(27), after a long stretch on how Prakṛti is separated from Puruṣa, on burning Prakṛti down day and night until it hides inside its source like fire in kindling, on the yogi who reaches Brahmā's world over many births.

Then: the yogi is separated from the *liṅga śarīra*. Then the siddhi clause. Then:

> When a person is not attached to these and does not pursue any other objective, he obtains me as a destination. **This is the infinite and death's laughter is not heard there.**[^1]

So the powers appear at the exact point where the account has run out of stages. Everything has been dissolved, the subtle body is gone, and the last remaining obstacle named is not a desire, a sin or an ignorance. It is a set of capacities the practice itself produced.

## Māyā Does Not Mean Fake Here

It is tempting to read *these are maya* as *these are illusions* — the powers do not really work, the yogi only thinks he flew.

The chapter will not carry that. Its own account of māyā, developed a few paragraphs earlier, is about a real thing seen wrongly: the sun is genuinely in the sky and its reflection is genuinely in the water, and the error is taking the reflection for the source.[^1] Nothing in the reflection is fake. What is false is the inference drawn from it.

So the siddhis are being placed on the reflection side. They occur, they are produced by the practice, and mistaking them for the thing the practice was for is the whole of the error.

**Which makes this a claim about attention rather than about physics.** The clause that follows says so directly — *when a person is not attached to these* — and the operative word is attachment, not disbelief. He is not asked to conclude the powers are unreal. He is asked to walk past them.

## The Eight, Named and Demoted

The volume names them, though not here. Debroy's note at 2(9) supplies the standard set: *aṇimā* (becoming as small as one wishes), *mahimā* (as large), *laghimā* (as light), *garimā* (as heavy), *prāpti* (obtaining what one wants), *prākāmya* (travelling where one wants), *vaśitvam* (control over creatures), *īśitvam* (divine powers).[^2]

And then the note's own verdict: *These are minor and temporary powers.*

Worth being precise about who is speaking. That assessment is the translator's, in an endnote, not the text's — the text at that point is discussing the lord's own powers and does not rank the eight at all.[^2] The judgement happens to agree with Kapila four hundred notes later, but it is apparatus, and this vault has learned to keep the two layers separate in this translator's work.[^3]

## Analytical Case Study: The Two Power Lists

Read the rest of that same note and something sharper appears.

> These are minor and temporary powers. **His personal powers are his knowledge, power, strength, prosperity, valour and energy.**[^2]

Eight powers on one side, six on the other. The eight are things you can *do* — shrink, expand, travel, control. The six are things you *are* — knowledge, strength, prosperity, valour.

**The eight are verbs and the six are attributes, and that is the whole distinction.** A capacity is something exercised on an occasion, which is why it can be minor and temporary; the six are not exercised, they are had, and nothing in the list has an occasion attached to it.

Which explains why the practice can produce the eight and never approach the six. You can train a capacity. The volume's own account of the six treats them as constitutive — what the illustrious one is made of rather than what he can perform.[^4]

And it explains Kapila's placement. The siddhis show up at the end of the dissolution sequence because they are the last thing the yogi can still *do*, and the destination he is described as obtaining is not a further capacity but a place: *he obtains me as a destination.*

## Not Forbidden — Enjoyed Elsewhere

The volume has already handled these powers once, two chapters earlier, and the handling is stranger than a prohibition:

> They do not desire the blissful prosperity of the illustrious one or the powers of the lord of maya. **Nor do they aspire for the eight kinds of siddhis. However, with me, the supreme one, they enjoy these in my world.**[^5]

So the devotees decline the eight and then have them anyway.

That is not a compromise or a reward for restraint — no causal link is offered, no *because they declined*. The two clauses simply sit next to each other: not aspired to, and enjoyed. The same shape the volume uses for the five liberations, where refusal and possession are described in one breath without the refusal being made into a technique for acquiring.[^6]

**The powers are not the problem. Wanting them is the problem, and the volume is entirely comfortable handing them to people who do not.**

## Where This Sits Among the Volume's Refusals

By this point in the ingest the pattern is familiar enough to name. The five liberations are offered and declined.[^6] The eight siddhis are available and walked past. Kuntī, offered relief, asks for the dangers to continue.[^7]

Three refusals with the same architecture: the thing is real, the thing is obtainable, the thing is on the table, and the text's interest is entirely in the person who did not want it.

What the siddhi clause adds is the sharpest version of the mechanism, because here the unwanted thing is *manufactured by the wanting-machine itself*. The liberations are offered by someone else. The siddhis are a by-product of the practice, which means the practitioner cannot avoid producing them and can only decline to be interested.

## Implementation Workflow: Walking Past What the Work Produces

You are deep in a long practice — a craft, a discipline, a business — and it has started throwing off capabilities you did not set out to acquire. You read a room fast now. You can produce the deliverable in a third of the time. People notice.

**Treat the by-products as evidence of position, not as the position.** They are real, they were produced by the work, and they are diagnostic in the way a temperature is diagnostic — informative and not the thing itself. Kapila does not tell the yogi they are worthless. He classifies them, which is a different act: he tells him what kind of object they are, so that they can be seen without being pursued.

**Watch for the point where the by-product becomes the deliverable.** This is the failure the placement warns about. The siddhis show up at the *end* of the sequence, when everything else has dissolved and they are the last available thing to do. That is exactly when a practitioner is most likely to reach for them — not early, when the work is obviously unfinished, but late, when there is nothing left to accomplish and a demonstrable capability is the only remaining way to feel like a practitioner.

**And do not try to prevent them.** The 3(25) passage is the useful note here: the powers arrive whether or not you wanted them, and refusing to develop them is not on offer. What is on offer is not being attached, which is a stance rather than an abstention, and a stance you can hold while the capability keeps accumulating.

## Evidence, Tensions, Open Questions

**The strongest evidence that this is a claim about attachment rather than about validity is the clause structure.** *There are siddhis obtained through yoga* concedes them entirely; the demotion arrives as a classification, and the operative instruction is *not attached to these*.

**Tension — the eight are declined at 3(25) and enjoyed in his world in the same sentence.** No mechanism connects the two, and the volume does not remark on it. **Preserved unresolved.**

**Tension — the demotion of the eight to *minor and temporary* is the translator's, at 2(9), not the text's.**[^2] Kapila's own verdict agrees but is differently framed — *these are maya*, which locates the error in the practitioner rather than in the powers' magnitude. **Preserved; the layers are kept apart.**

**Open question.** The siddhis are named nowhere in the Kapila discourse itself — the list comes from an endnote four hundred notes earlier. Does the text of Volume 1 ever enumerate the eight in its own voice?[^8]

## Author Tensions & Convergences

The vault's Gauḍīya layer treats the siddhis the way it treats the liberations: as a category of temptation with a settled ranking, subordinate to *prema* and generally handled through the logic of *anyābhilāṣitā-śūnyam* — devotion emptied of other desires, with mystic powers listed among the other desires.

Kapila does not run that argument, and the difference is in the framing rather than the verdict. His term is *māyā*, not *anartha* — a classification of what kind of thing the powers are, not a warning about what they will do to you. The later tradition's version tells the practitioner the siddhis are a hazard. The primary text tells him they are a reflection, and lets the practical conclusion follow on its own.

The convergence is real and the register is not the same, which is the pattern this build keeps finding at the junction between the source and its systematisation.

## Cross-Domain Handshakes

**With [[ARCHIVES/concepts/psychology/spiritual-bypass-and-pitfalls|Spiritual Bypass and Pitfalls]].** That page holds the clinical version: contemplative practice reliably produces states, insights and capacities that get recruited to avoid the developmental work the practice was supposed to support — equanimity used to skip grief, insight used to skip repair, and the practitioner's genuine attainments functioning as the material of the evasion.

Kapila's clause is the same structural observation without the pathology. The practice produces real capacities; the capacities are where the practitioner gets stuck; the sticking is not caused by anything going wrong.

**What the pairing produces:** the clinical framing treats bypass as a misuse — something has been diverted, and the remedy is to notice the diversion and return to the neglected work. Kapila's placement suggests the diversion is not optional and not a symptom. The siddhis arrive at the terminus of the sequence, after the subtle body has gone, when there is nothing left to accomplish. On that reading, the by-product problem is not a failure of the practitioner's honesty but a structural feature of any practice that outlives its own goals: the discipline keeps producing capability after it has stopped producing progress, and the capability is the only thing still visible.

Which is testable outside contemplative settings, and it predicts something the clinical frame does not — that the highest-risk moment for a long practice is not early enthusiasm but late competence, and that the practitioners most likely to substitute their powers for their purpose are the ones with the most powers and the least remaining to do.

## The Live Edge

**Sharpest implication.** *There are siddhis* concedes the powers completely and *these are maya* reclassifies them, which makes the ruling an instruction about attention rather than a claim about efficacy — the yogi is not asked to disbelieve what his practice produced, only to walk past it. And the placement is the argument: the powers surface at the end of the dissolution sequence, when they are the last thing a practitioner can still do, which is exactly when doing something is most tempting.

**Generative questions.**

1. The eight are declined at 3(25) and enjoyed in his world in the next clause. Is there any passage where that adjacency is explained rather than stated?
2. Eight capacities against six attributes. Does the volume anywhere treat the six as attainable, or are they constitutive throughout?
3. The siddhi clause closes 3(27) and is never returned to. Does any narrative in the four Skandhas show a figure stuck at exactly this point?

# The Six Completion-Stage Yogas

## Six Rungs, and Three of Them Are Called "Isolation"

Here is a ladder whose rungs have strange names:

> the Completion Stage of Tantra is actually divided into six separate yogas, which in ascending order are called the stages of:
> **1. Physical Isolation · 2. Verbal Isolation · 3. Mental Isolation · 4. Attainment of the Impure Illusory Body · 5. Actual Clear Light · 6. Learner's Union**[^1]

*Isolation* three times, and then three things that sound like results rather than exercises.

The word is doing something specific and it is worth getting right before anything else. To *isolate* here does not mean to withdraw from the world. It means to **decouple a faculty from its ordinary automatic operation** — to get the body, then the voice-and-breath, then the discriminating mind, running free of the habitual couplings that normally drive them.

Three decouplings, then three arrivals. That is the shape.

## Where Each Rung Lands

Bodri's whole comparative project is mapping schemes onto one another, and he maps this one:

> Of these particular yogas or practice levels, **the Tantric stage of Clear Light Attainment corresponds to the great event of Seeing the Tao.** … **The Tantric Stage of Learner's Union therefore matches with the Mahayana Stage of Cultivating the Path**, for it means you're in union with the true essence of the path and know how you should proceed in practice.[^1]

So the six-rung ladder is not six steps to enlightenment. It is:

- **Rungs 1–4** — everything before the threshold.
- **Rung 5** — the threshold itself. Seeing the Tao.
- **Rung 6** — the beginning of the far side.

Which relocates the ladder's centre of gravity dramatically. Two thirds of the named rungs sit in preparation, one is the event, and one covers the entire remainder of the path — the part this book elsewhere says is longer than everything preceding it.

Bodri is candid that the mapping is the hard part: *"The only difficulty in making these large scale correspondences lies in partitioning the Tantric Completion Stage Yogas into discrete phases that correspond to the separate stages of Preparatory Yoga Practices, Seeing the Tao, and True Cultivation Practice."*[^1] He states the difficulty and then performs the match anyway, in two sentences, with no argument for the alignment beyond its plausibility.

## What You Actually Do on the First Three Rungs

The practices attached to the isolations are named, and the pairing is tidy:

> **Deity yoga**, for instance, is stressed at the stage of **Physical Isolation** for the task of preliminarily cultivating the jing, chi and mai, whereas **mantra practice** is stressed at the stage of **Verbal Isolation** to further cultivate the chi, hsi and the calming of the sixth consciousness.[^2]

Visual practice for the body. Sound practice for the breath and voice. And the third:

> Because you can cultivate your chi at the stage of Body Isolation, and cut off the sixth consciousness through the practices of Verbal Isolation, then you can finally attain a degree of mental emptiness whereby **the mind is isolated from normal mundane mentality** … All this activity gives rise to the stage that the Esoteric school calls **Mental Isolation.** In this stage of Tantra you're cultivating your chi and shen, so **upon reaching it you're on the very border of genuine samadhi attainments.**[^2]

Note the sequence is *dependent*, not merely ordered. Mental Isolation is described as a consequence of the first two rather than as a separate technique — you do not practise it, you arrive at it.

And Bodri's summary judgement on the whole scheme, delivered flatly:

> these three initial stages of the Tantric path can be seen as **simply another way to partition the normal process of cultivation** that you've already become familiar with through a variety of other partitioning schemes.[^2]

Another partition. Not another path.

## A Second Partition, Also Tsong Khapa's

Then, eleven pages later, the same author introduces a *different* division of the same completion stage:

> the great Tibetan master Tsong Khapa summarized for us **an entirely different approach to the Completion Stage Yogas that follows the Six Yogas of Naropa tradition.**[^3]

Two six-fold schemes of the same territory, both authoritative, both Tibetan, and Bodri prints them without reconciling them. He offers a reason for including the second — *"it once again illustrates the same basic principles"* — which is a claim about their agreement in spirit, not about how their rungs correspond.

The Naropa scheme's organising principle is different in kind. Where the isolations partition by *faculty* — body, voice, mind — the Naropa scheme partitions by *technique*, and it has a named foundation:

> In this tradition the expression **"the inner heat, the foundation,"** is well known. This is because in the completion stage yogas one uses the inner heat technology from the very beginning in order to collect the subtle life-sustaining energies into the central channel … **This is the actual basis upon which all practices rely, and upon which all later completion stage yogas are founded.**[^4]

Everything rests on tumo. And the prerequisite is stated as non-negotiable: *"all systems of highest yoga tantra's completion stage involve the preliminary process of controlling the vital energies flowing through the two side channels … and redirecting them into the central channel, avadhuti. **This is indispensable.**"*[^4]

## You Cannot Get Oil by Crushing Sand

Inside that passage sits the sharpest exchange in the tantric chapters, and it is aimed directly at people who meditate well.

Tsong Khapa first states the negative case:

> if one does not rely upon a profound path of this nature … but instead **engages a samadhi that merely maintains a state of non-conceptual absorption for a prolonged period of time, no great signs of progress will be produced.**[^4]

Bodri's own bracketed gloss on that line reads *[this is dry Zen or dead Zen, a stage of clear equanimity without the circulation of the vital force]* — and it is his interpolation, not Tsong Khapa's.[^4]

Then the story:

> when Milarepa and Gampopa met for the first time and Gampopa commented that **he could sit in meditative concentration for many days at a time without distraction**, Milarepa replied to him, **"You cannot get oil by crushing sand. The practice of samadhi is not sufficient in and of itself."**[^4]

Days of unbroken concentration, and the answer is: *that is sand.*

This is a serious claim and it cuts against a great deal of what this book argues elsewhere. Bodri's general position is that samādhi is the currency of the path — *samādhi is the only real discipline*, absorptions are merit achievements, the ladder of the nine is the spine of the whole corpus. Here a founder-figure of the tradition he is summarising says prolonged absorption on its own yields *no great signs of progress.*

The reconciliation available is that Milarepa is distinguishing *kinds* of samādhi — absorption with the energies in the central channel, against absorption without — which is exactly the biconditional the book asserts elsewhere. On that reading Gampopa's days of concentration simply were not samādhi in the technical sense, however they felt.

But notice what that costs. **If a practitioner can sit undistracted for days and still be crushing sand, then subjective steadiness is not a reliable indicator of anything**, and the practitioner has no internal way to tell which kind they have. The scheme's own diagnostic — the four signs, the blisses — is the only check, and it is available only after the transition it is meant to verify.

## The Ladder Is Not a Technology

Before either scheme is introduced, Bodri plants a constraint that both have to satisfy, and it is easy to skip because it reads like piety:

> **you cannot avoid the necessity of cultivating this moral basis if you want to make progress. After all, the samadhi are basically merit achievements**, so you need merit in order to advance to these great spiritual states. In other words, **you cannot escape the need for moral training in spirituality — it is never ever divorced from the path.**[^6]

*The samādhi are basically merit achievements.* That is a strong claim and it is the one that stops the whole tantric apparatus from being a machine.

If absorption were purely technological — energies, channels, heat, retention — then it would be available to anyone who ran the protocol correctly, in the way that a chemical reaction is available to anyone with the reagents. This sentence denies that. The rungs are gated by something the protocol cannot supply.

He gives three worked routes to the merit, and their diversity is the interesting part: **Marpa** accumulated it by making large offerings for the teachings; others by generosity and charity; **Milarepa and Naropa** by suffering so severely that *"(in relative proportion) their bad karma was burned away and past merits could manifest leading to insight into the Tao."*[^6]

Payment, service, or suffering. Three currencies, one account.

And the balancing clause, so this does not collapse into moralism: *"Merit, of course, is absolutely necessary but rarely sufficient by itself"* — you need prajñā too, and the old formula he quotes is *"great virtue and great wisdom produce great success."*[^6]

Which sets a test the two six-rung schemes both fail to address. **Neither ladder has a rung for merit.** The isolations are faculties; the Naropa yogas are techniques. The one ingredient declared indispensable appears in neither enumeration — which means a practitioner working either scheme can be doing everything the map shows and still be missing the thing the map's author says is required.

## Implementation Workflow

You have got good at sitting. An hour is easy, distraction is rare, and the quiet is genuinely deep.

The passage above is aimed at you, and its message is unwelcome: this may be sand.

The test the scheme offers is not about the quality of the quiet. It is about whether anything is *moving.* Warmth at the navel that arises rather than being imagined. The signs, in order — mirage, smoke, fireflies, lamp. A change in the breath that happens to you rather than one you produce. If none of that has ever occurred across years of excellent sitting, the tradition's reading is that you have been maintaining a state rather than undergoing a process.

What it does *not* license is panic or a change of school. Bodri's own repeated advice, and the Zen position he keeps returning to, is that the energies enter the channel by themselves once the sixth consciousness settles — so the correct response to a long plateau is not to bolt on a forcing technique.

The honest middle, held from both sides: keep sitting, and stop treating steadiness as the score. Steadiness is the condition under which something else may happen. It is not the something else.

Months later there is a subtler version of the same trap. A sign arrives — real warmth, an unmistakable change — and the mind immediately reaches for the ladder. *Which rung is this?* Two schemes are available, they partition differently, and both are in the same book. The reaching is the sixth consciousness resuming exactly the work the first two isolations were for.

## Analytical Case Study: Two Ladders, One Stairwell

The methodological problem here is worth stating plainly, because it is the book's own method turned on itself.

Bodri's comparative project rests on a claim: different traditions partition one process differently, and once you see the correspondences you see the process. That claim is defended across hundreds of pages, and it is largely persuasive when the traditions are distant — Taoist, Christian, yogic.

Here the two schemes are **not distant.** Both are Tibetan. Both are completion-stage. Both are attributed to Tsong Khapa in this very book — the six isolations are given as the Tantric completion stage's structure, and eleven pages later Tsong Khapa is credited with *"an entirely different approach"* following Naropa.

And they are not reconciled. There is no table, no mapping, no statement of which rung of one corresponds to which of the other.

That absence is significant for three reasons.

**It is the easiest case the method will ever face.** Same tradition, same century, same named authority, same subject matter. If the correspondences cannot be drawn here, the confidence with which they are drawn between Zen and Kabbalah is unearned.

**The book notices the difficulty in the general case and skips it in the specific one.** *"The only difficulty in making these large scale correspondences lies in partitioning the Tantric Completion Stage Yogas into discrete phases"* — that sentence names precisely the work this section then does not do.[^1]

**And the two schemes disagree about what the completion stage is organised by.** Faculty, or technique. One says the ladder is body, voice, mind. The other says the ladder is inner heat and what inner heat makes possible. Those are different answers to *what varies as you ascend*, and a reader holding both has two incompatible pictures of their own progress.

The right handling: **carry both, mapped to neither.** This vault's page for each names its own organising axis and states that the source prints them side by side without reconciliation. That matches the standing rule against silently resolving contradictions, and it is also simply what the evidence supports.

## Evidence, Tensions, Open Questions

**Strongest support: the six isolations are enumerated cleanly and their organising principle is legible.** Three decouplings by faculty, then three arrivals, with the threshold explicitly at rung five.[^1]

**Second: the practices attached to the first two rungs are specified and the third is derived rather than practised.** That internal dependency is a real structural claim, not a list.[^2]

**Third: the Milarepa rebuke is unusually costly to the book's own emphasis** and is printed anyway.[^4]

**Tension, unresolved and the largest in the cluster: two six-fold partitions of the same stage, both Tibetan, both credited to Tsong Khapa, printed eleven pages apart with no correspondence drawn.**[^1][^3]

**Tension: if days of undistracted concentration can be sand, subjective steadiness indicates nothing** — and the scheme's only check becomes available after the transition it verifies.[^4]

**Open question.** Rung six, Learner's Union, covers the entire far side of the threshold in one word. What are its internal divisions? The Naropa scheme does not supply them either. **The most detailed technical vocabulary in the corpus stops at the exact point where the corpus says most of the work begins** — and no reason is given in the range read (pp 542, 550–555).

## Author Tensions & Convergences

[[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/generation-and-completion|Generation and Completion]] supplies the two-stage frame this ladder subdivides, and reading them together produces the asymmetry neither states: **the generation stage — where every beginner spends years — gets one paragraph and a list of five activities, while the completion stage gets two competing six-rung schemes.** The mapping is finest where fewest people are standing, which is a property of the literature rather than of the path.

Against [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/samadhi-is-the-only-real-discipline|Samādhi Is the Only Real Discipline]], the Milarepa passage is a direct strain and it is worth not smoothing. That page carries Bodri's insistence that samādhi is the currency of everything. This one carries a founder-figure telling a man who can sit undistracted for days that he is crushing sand. Both are in the same book; the reconciliation — that only channel-entered absorption counts — is available and is never stated at the point of collision.

And against [[ARCHIVES/concepts/creative-practice/repetition-as-a-deliberate-method|Repetition as a Deliberate Method]] there is an odd mirror worth recording. That page carries this same author defending his own repetition as method rather than defect: the same claims returning in different clothes, deliberately. **The two six-rung schemes are that habit at the level of structure** — the same territory presented twice in different vocabularies. Whether that is method or defect depends entirely on whether the second presentation is mapped to the first, and here it is not.

## Cross-Domain Handshakes

*One handshake below. The Milarepa material invited a second — practice quantity against practice quality — but the honest reading is that nothing in the vault yet carries that argument at the level of mechanism, and a connection asserted without one is decoration.*

### Behavioral Mechanics: Watchers, Listeners, Touchers

The sensory-mode framework holds that people process through a dominant channel — visual, auditory-verbal, or kinaesthetic — and that under stress most drift to their primary. The tactical application is *matching*: pitch to a Watcher in images, to a Listener in language, to a Toucher in sensation and movement.[^5]

Now look at the first three rungs. **Physical Isolation, worked through deity yoga — a visualisation practice. Verbal Isolation, worked through mantra — a sound practice. Mental Isolation, arrived at rather than practised.** Visual, then verbal, then the mind decoupled once the first two are running.

The correspondence is at the level of the channels themselves, and it is close enough to be surprising: a fifteenth-century Tibetan curriculum and a modern influence framework carve human processing into substantially the same modalities.

What the pairing produces is a genuine methodological disagreement, and it is the useful part. **The influence framework says match the channel to the person. The tantric curriculum says run all three, in a fixed order, on everybody.**

Both are defensible and they are optimising different things. Matching is right when you need an effect *now*, in one encounter, with someone whose defaults you must work with — that is the operator's problem. Sequencing is right when you are building a *capability* over years, and where the person's weak channels are precisely the ones that need work — that is the trainer's problem. A Watcher who is never made to do mantra practice keeps a decoupled body and a coupled voice.

The insight neither field states: **a persuasion technology and a training technology will always recommend opposite things about individual difference**, because one exploits the existing configuration and the other is trying to change it. Which supplies a fast test for any practice tradition that starts offering personalised paths — *are you being matched to your strengths, or is that just easier to sell?*

## The Live Edge

**Sharpest implication.** A practitioner who can sit undistracted for days may have nothing, and cannot tell from inside — because the scheme's only diagnostic becomes available at the transition it exists to verify. **Every internal report of progress is uninformative by the tradition's own account, and it says this while selling a ladder.**

**Generative questions.**

If the six isolations are "simply another way to partition the normal process," what would falsify a partition? Two schemes carve the same stretch differently and both are held to be correct. At what point does a partitioning scheme make a claim rather than offer a vocabulary?

And: why does the technical detail stop dead at Learner's Union? The obvious answer — that almost nobody has been there to report — would apply equally to Actual Clear Light, which gets specified in fine grain.

## Connected Concepts

- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/generation-and-completion|Generation and Completion]] — the two-stage frame this ladder subdivides
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/samadhi-is-the-only-real-discipline|Samādhi Is the Only Real Discipline]] — the position the Milarepa rebuke strains
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/samadhi-only-when-chi-is-in-the-central-channel|Samādhi Only When Chi Is in the Central Channel]] — the biconditional that makes "crushing sand" coherent
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/the-four-descending-and-ascending-blisses|The Four Descending and Ascending Blisses]] — the inner-heat protocol this scheme rests on, with the manuals' omissions
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/eastern-spirituality/the-esoteric-schools-vocabulary-decoded|The Esoteric Schools' Vocabulary Decoded]] — what the rung names turn out to mean
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/creative-practice/repetition-as-a-deliberate-method|Repetition as a Deliberate Method]] — the same author's habit, at the level of structure
- [[ARCHIVES/concepts/behavioral-mechanics/watchers-listeners-touchers-sensory-mode-classification|Watchers, Listeners, Touchers]] — the same three channels, sequenced instead of matched
